introduction: The Báb spent much of his short ministry preparing his followers for someone else, and these prayers show the anxiety of it. He asks that the people of the Bayán be rained on with help, purified, protected, and above all kept from doing to the next Messenger what he had seen done to himself. The last reading is Bahá’u’lláh’s, after many of them had turned away, and it is still a prayer for them. The nearest parallels are the prayers of Jesus for his disciples and for those who rejected him, John the Baptist’s “he must increase,” and Moses’s two ways. Paul adds a caution to any new community that looks back on an older one, and his “the letter killeth” stands beside the Báb’s care for every point of his book.
questions: The Báb prays that his followers will not “pronounce censure” against the One to come. What makes it hard for people who waited faithfully to recognize what they waited for?
“I have not witnessed among the people of Islam a goodly upbringing that would manifest Thy love.” How does Paul’s “boast not against the branches” guard against reading this with self-satisfaction?
Every letter of the Bayán is to be preserved, and yet some are blamed for clinging to letters. Where is the line between faithfulness to a text and bondage to it?
Bahá’u’lláh prays for the people who turned away from him. What does that example, with Jesus’s “Father, forgive them,” ask of someone who has been rejected?

outside.why: The Báb, his mission delivered, asks that his own people be guarded “on that Day.” Jesus on the night before his death: I pray for them; keep through thine own name those whom thou hast given me.
The fear is that they will “pronounce censure” against the One to come. Jesus to Peter before the denial: I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not.
A prayer for “the rain of Thy triumph” upon a people. Isaiah uses rain for what God sends that does not fail: as the rain cometh down and watereth the earth, so shall my word be.
“Purify all the mirrors of hearts.” David’s prayer for his own: create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.
The fire of negation or the paradise of affirmation. Moses sets the same two ways before a people about to cross over: life and death, blessing and cursing; therefore choose life.

A whole people waited and wept through long nights, and when the day came “I witnessed no servants who would praise Thee … or thank Thee.” Jesus, after ten were healed and one came back: where are the nine?
The Báb prays that his followers will do better at the next coming. John’s prologue states what he fears: he came unto his own, and his own received him not.

“I have not witnessed among the people of Islam a goodly upbringing.” Paul, writing of the people who had not received his message, warns the newer community: boast not against the branches; thou bearest not the root, but the root thee. Does the Báb’s prayer for his own people carry the same warning?
Preserve whoever preserves the Bayán, “even to a single point.” Jesus of the Law: one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass, till all be fulfilled.

Whoever fails to keep a single point is to be cast away. Paul: the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life. The last reading describes people “clinging to the letters of their own selves.” How can a scripture be kept to the letter without that?
The Bayán and its followers are “but a present” to Him Whom God shall make manifest, who may dismiss them all. John the Baptist of the one who came after him: he must increase, but I must decrease.
Bahá’u’lláh sees that the people of the Bayán “have turned away,” and prays for them. Jesus beheld the city and wept over it: if thou hadst known the things which belong unto thy peace!
A prayer for those who dispute the verses. From the cross: Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do.
